item.title: OGLE Pre-discovery Observations of the Dwarf Planet Candidate 2026 ED138
item.description: arXiv:2611.15959v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The newly discovered trans-Neptunian object, 2026 ED138, is a strong dwarf planet candidate detected by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Despite its high intrinsic brightness, it evaded detection by previous sky surveys as it hid near crowded Galactic disk fields. Here, we present an analysis of precovery observations of 2026 ED138 in archival data from the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE). We identify 102 reliable detections of the object as it moved across the dense regions of the Galactic plane and bulge between 2011 and 2024. We provide precise astrometric and photometric measurements of the object. Modeling its phase curve yields absolute magnitudes of H_I = 2.224 +/- 0.034 mag and H_V = 3.154 +/- 0.035 mag. Period analysis of the phase-angle-corrected light curve reveals a candidate rotation period of 1.18077 days and its 1-day alias 0.54066 days, although a low signal-to-noise ratio renders these periodicities tentative.
item.dc:creator: P. Mr\'oz, A. Udalski, I. Soszy\'nski, M. K. Szyma\'nski, P. Pietrukowicz, R. Poleski, J. Skowron, K. Ulaczyk, M. Gromadzki, K. Rybicki, P. Iwanek, M. Wrona, M. J. Mr\'oz

item.title: Crater Scaling Relationships for Gas Impingement on Planetary Regolith
item.description: arXiv:2611.16040v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Plume-surface interaction (PSI) effects remains a major uncertainty for operations on regolith-covered planetary bodies. Although spacecraft exhaust can erode surfaces, form craters, and accelerate ejecta, existing PSI relationships are largely derived for scenario-specific lunar and Martian landing conditions and are not yet reliably generalizable. Resolving this problem is important not only for spacecraft safety, but also because controlled thruster interactions could provide an active geotechnical experiment during asteroid reconnaissance. Measurements of thruster-formed craters and ejecta may constrain regolith density, strength, porosity, and particle properties that are otherwise difficult to determine remotely. Such information is particularly relevant to planetary defense, where uncertainty in near-surface properties can strongly affect the outcome of kinetic-impact mitigation and the interpretation of momentum transfer. We investigate gas-driven excavation using near-vacuum, pulsed-N$_2$ experiments in a cohesionless asteroid regolith analog and comparisons with a low-gravity drop-tower experiment and historical chemical-thruster tests. We adapt projectile-cratering $\pi$-scaling, and find that these relationships can describe gas crater volume as a function of gas, target, gravity, and nozzle properties. A common gravity-regime relationship describes the laboratory data and is consistent with an experimental low-gravity result. Generalizing the $\pi$-scaling relationship for cohesive targets shows consistency with Apollo-era chemical-thruster cases. These results provide a framework for using spacecraft thrusters as active geotechnical tools during small-body reconnaissance.
item.dc:creator: Ronald-L. Ballouz, Olivier S. Barnouin, Mitsuhisa Baba, Vicki L. Toy-Edens, Noble Hatten, Parvathy Prem, Maarij Qureshi, Cecily Sunday

item.title: A Bright L4 Neptune Trojan Found by Stacking Archival ZTF Images
item.description: arXiv:2611.16046v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report a Neptune Trojan found by a shift-and-stack search of archival Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) difference images of 2019 October, and recovered in public images of seven other telescopes back to 2008. The orbit uses 88 positions on 54 nights from 2008 to 2025, a 17.22-year arc, all measured on our own Gaia DR3 plate solutions. Its heliocentric osculating elements at JD 2460000.5 are a = 30.2158 +/- 0.0004 au, e = 0.0661 and i = 20.32 deg; a fit of the same positions with the independent orbit code Find_Orb agrees within 0.4 sigma in every element. The nominal orbit librates about Neptune's leading Lagrange point L4 with a period of 9.25 kyr and an amplitude of 8.7 deg over the next Myr, and 84 +/- 2% of 500 clones of the orbit remain L4 Trojans for 4.5 Gyr. Its absolute magnitude is H_V = 6.96 +/- 0.10 (linear phase law), or 6.81 +/- 0.06 on the H, G convention of the Minor Planet Center's list of Neptune Trojans, whose brightest L4 member has H = 7.26, so the object is possibly the brightest known L4 Neptune Trojan. Its color, g-r = 0.52 +/- 0.05, lies in the g-r range of the red Neptune Trojans, and for albedos of 0.05-0.15 its diameter is about 140-240 km.
item.dc:creator: Jorrit B. Jongma

item.title: The ZTF Variability Archive (ZVAR): Initial Data Release (DR1)
item.description: arXiv:2611.16166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) has observed the northern sky observable from Palomar Observatory since March 2018, accumulating a median of a thousand photometric measurements across $gri$ for each of more than a billion sources. Among these billions of objects are millions of periodically variable stars, active galactic nuclei, stellar remnants, and substellar objects. We describe the initial data release (DR1) of the ZTF Variability Archive (ZVAR) which provides image difference forced photometry, candidate periods, and variability metrics for approximately 1.3 billion sources in ZTF having an identification in Pan-STARRS1 DR1 (PS1). The data cover the 5.37 year interval between March 2018 and July 2023. ZVAR is sensitive to periods between 5 minutes and 2.7 years. We also describe tools for accessing the ZVAR data.
item.dc:creator: Matthew J. Graham, Samuel Whitebook, Andrew J. Drake, Thomas Prince, Thomas Culino, Ilaria Caiazzo, Jan van Roestel, Zach Vanderbosch, Theo du Laz, Przemek Mroz, Kevin Burdge

item.title: C$_2$ Swan, CH and CN emission, surface temperature and luminous efficiency of the Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule from ground-based spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.16291v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule entered the atmosphere over South Australia on 5 December 2020 at 12 km/s. A slitless spectral video, taken from the ground with a hand-tracked consumer camera, shows the capsule alone from 80 to 49 km. In the first ten seconds of heating the shock layer emits the CN violet system, the CH A-X band and the C$_2$ Swan bands, the latter for the first time in remote observations of a capsule entry. C$_2$ ($T_{\rm rot}\approx9200$ K, $T_{\rm vib}\approx7800$ K) and CN (about 7000 K) are far hotter than the surface. C$_2$ and CH disappear while the heat flux is still rising and CN persists, which we relate to the early pyrolysis of the carbon-phenolic ablator and to the changing boundary-layer chemistry. The colour temperature of the heat shield rises from 2720 to 3080 K, in agreement with airborne results. The radiated energy is one to two orders of magnitude below that of natural fireballs, because the light comes from the hot surface rather than from ablation vapour. A faint persistent train lights up about 1 s after the passage and fades within a few seconds, probably chemiluminescence in the cooling wake.
item.dc:creator: Shinsuke Abe, Hadrien A. R. Devillepoix, Eleanor K. Sansom, Masa-yuki Yamamoto, Satoshi Tanaka, Yoshiaki Ishihara, Kazuhisa Fujita, Makoto Yoshikawa, Martin C. Towner, Martin Cup\'ak, Kei-ichi Okuyama, Takumi Ogawa, Amane Uda, Satoshi Nozawa, Yoshihiro Hiramatsu, Taichi Kawamura, Norihisa Segawa, Yoshihiro Kakinami, Andrew Cool, Geoffrey Bonning, Hirohide Demura

item.title: Self-Organizing Maps for the Exploration and Classification of X-Ray Sources in the Chandra Source Catalog
item.description: arXiv:2611.16539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we apply Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to the Chandra Source Catalog (CSC) to investigate the distribution of observation-level detections in the feature space defined by their spectral and variability properties. SOMs are neural-network-based models that project points in high-dimensional space onto a two-dimensional latent space while preserving their local topological structure. From CSC 2.1.1 we extract a sample of 36,904 ACIS-only, observation-level, high statistical significance detections, belonging to 17,927 unique sources. Among these detections, 25,192 (10,078 sources) are associated with a label from SIMBAD via a 1" cross-match that provides information about their astrophysical nature. Training a 40x40 hexagonal SOM reveals structured regions in the U-Matrix and activation response map, and feature-projection maps trace coherent patterns in spectral shape and variability. Overlaying SIMBAD classes shows that labeled populations occupy distinct, partially adjacent regions of the map and that generic categories can be interpreted via their SOM locations. We then retrain the SOM for classification using a source-grouped train/validation/test split and introduce SOMClassifier. When applied to 11,712 detections without SIMBAD labels, it assigns valid (non-abstained) labels to 6,225 detections (coverage ~53%). Furthermore, we release the trained models and visualization/classification workflows through a public web application built on the most up-to-date CSC release.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Scaudo, Raffaele D'Abrusco, V. Samuel P\'erez-D\'iaz, Juan Rafael Mart\'inez-Galarza, Marco Landoni

item.title: Mitigating variance shrinkage in multi-task galaxy property inference from imaging data via statistical manifold alignment
item.description: arXiv:2611.16598v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inferring photometric redshifts ($z$) and key stellar population properties ($\log(M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot)$, $D_n4000$, and $\mathrm{H}\delta_A$) directly from multi-band imaging is increasingly critical for spectroscopically limited large surveys such as LSST and CSST. However, conventional point-wise loss functions (e.g., mean squared error or Huber loss) employed in deep neural networks often induce ``variance shrinkage''---a regression-to-the-mean effect that contracts predicted variances, distorts non-linear physical manifolds (such as bimodal distributions), and truncates heavy-tail populations. Here, we present ViTMultiTask, a vision transformer framework that incorporates a multi-scale maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss to enforce higher-order joint distribution alignment in reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Trained on 83,846 galaxies from Subaru HSC five-band ($g,r,i,z,y$) imaging cross-matched with DESI Data Release 1 Bright Galaxy Survey spectra, the model achieves high point-estimate precision on an independent test set of 5,000 galaxies: $\sigma_{\mathrm{NMAD}} = 0.020$ for $z$, $0.169\,\mathrm{dex}$ for $\log(M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot)$, $0.073$ for $D_n4000$, and $1.185\,\text{\r{A}}$ for $\mathrm{H}\delta_A$. Ablation experiments demonstrate that incorporating the MMD loss effectively mitigates variance shrinkage and more accurately reproduces the observed spectroscopic parameter distributions (including bimodal structures and heavy tails), while maintaining point-estimate accuracy statistically consistent with the baseline (RMSE changes $\le 3.5\%$) and catastrophic outlier rates fully comparable to the baseline. This kernel-based manifold alignment offers a statistically grounded and practical paradigm for comprehensive galaxy property inference in the deep imaging era.
item.dc:creator: Zhijian Luo, Jianzhen Chen

item.title: Active Learning for Molecular Discovery: A Retrospective Test toward TMC-1
item.description: arXiv:2611.16741v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine-learning recommendation lists can help prioritize searches for new interstellar molecules, but whether reranking such a list as detections accumulate improves on it has not been tested. We present a pre-registered retrospective test toward TMC-1, using a published machine-learning list of 1,510 recommended candidates, consolidated to 1,434 candidates, and the species reported there through September 2026. At four annual origins from 2022 to 2025, a logistic-regression ranking on seven released features, refit on the detections known at each origin, separates later detections from never-detected candidates with a pooled AUC of 0.867, against 0.706 for the best single-criterion baseline (difference 0.160; 95\% interval 0.095-0.230). The advantage persists under a shifted date boundary and two alternative feature regimes, but is not established among the top 100 candidates (12 versus 7 detections). A searcher that refits on its own observations reaches half of the 63 detected species on the list in a median of 200 observations, against 332 for the best fixed ordering and 717.5 expected for random search. Uncertainty sampling, the standard active-learning rule, performs worse than random (AUC 0.210): later detections lie at low predictive uncertainty, close to known chemistry. Of 101 species in our validation set, 37 are absent from the list, and only 13 of these appear in a pool rebuilt from its source databases, including 2 of 11 radicals and neither ion. Candidate generation, not ranking, is the main constraint. We release 100 recommended targets, with code and frozen inputs, for prospective testing.
item.dc:creator: R. I. El-Kholy, Z. M. Hayman

item.title: Combining TTVs, RVs, and astrometry to characterize distant giant companions of transiting hot Jupiters: Application to WASP-4
item.description: arXiv:2611.16782v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The origins and architectures of hot Jupiter (HJ) systems remain unclear, with potential explanations for the tight orbits being in-situ formation, disk-migration, or high-eccentricity migration. These mechanisms can leave different imprints on the orbital architecture, but tidal interactions act to erase these imprints for HJs, leading to orbital circularization, realignment, and potentially orbital decay. The latter can be mimicked by the introduction of light travel-time effects (LTTE) caused by an outer giant companion, as for WASP-4$\,$b. We examine the WASP-4 system using newly obtained ESO$\,$3.6/HARPS radial velocity (RV) observations and archival transit-timing data, leveraging the LTTE. Furthermore, we present a novel approach of analyzing HJ systems in sight of $\textit{Gaia}$'s Data Release 4. We propose combining RV, transit-timing, and astrometry data, making use of the LTTE as a proxy for the orbital motion of a possible outer companion. We combine and fit all currently available data and simulate $\textit{Gaia}$ DR4 and DR5 astrometric measurements of WASP-4 and perform an injection and recovery procedure to estimate their impact on the recovered planetary parameters of WASP-4$\,$c. The procedure employs a combined model that describes RVs, transit timing variations (TTVs) via the LTTE, and astrometry simultaneously. Analyzing the existing data, we improve the planetary parameters of WASP-4$\,$c, finding a minimum mass of $9.3\pm1.7\,M_\mathrm{Jup}$ with an orbital period of $10\,600^{+1100}_{-1000}\,$d, or about $29\,$yr. Furthermore, we find that there is no significant orbital decay taking place for WASP-4$\,$b. In simulations of $\textit{Gaia}$ DR5, our three-pronged approach reduces the error bars of WASP-4$\,$c's parameters by about $10\%$, $25\%$, and $33\%$ for its orbital period, time of inferior conjunction, and RV semi-amplitude, respectively. (abridged)
item.dc:creator: J. -V. Harre, Louise D. Nielsen, A. M. S. Smith

item.title: Rapid Multiparameter Gravitational-Wave Tests of General Relativity with Neural Posterior Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.17038v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiparameter gravitational-wave tests of general relativity (GR) are limited by strong correlations among post-Newtonian (PN) phase deformations and the computational cost of Bayesian inference. We present DINGO-TGR, a neural posterior estimation framework that jointly infers binary-source parameters and six PN phase deformations within the TIGER parametrization, using IMRPhenomXPHM waveforms with spin precession and higher-order modes. Importance sampling reweights the neural proposal samples, while principal component analysis (PCA) identifies two well-constrained combinations of PN deformations. We validate the framework using 16 zero-noise GR injections and 12 beyond-GR injections, recovering GR-consistent posteriors in the former and leading-mode shifts consistent with the injected deformations in the latter. For GW150914 and GW250114, our results agree with independent \texttt{bilby-tgr} analyses using \texttt{dynesty}. After training, inference including importance sampling takes approximately 38 minutes and 4.4 hours, respectively, compared with 177 and 238 hours for conventional sampling. GW150914 exhibits a mild offset from GR in the leading PCA mode, whereas GW250114 is consistent with GR. To assess the significance of the GW150914 offset, we analyze 1000 GW150914-like GR injections with independent Gaussian-noise realizations and fixed detector power spectral densities. The resulting empirical upper-tail $p$-value is $11.5\%$, indicating that the observed offset does not reject the adopted GR null model at the 5\% significance level. Our results demonstrate the potential of importance-sampling-corrected neural inference for efficient multiparameter GR tests and large-scale injection-based significance assessments.
item.dc:creator: Hong Su, Tao Yang, He Wang

item.title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers
item.description: arXiv:2611.17052v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.
item.dc:creator: \'I\~nigo Zubeldia, Boris Bolliet, Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Pablo Villanueva-Domingo, Miles Cranmer

item.title: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope: Passband Measurements with an Analysis of Systematic Errors
item.description: arXiv:2608.18348v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present measurements of the spectral response of the four Advanced ACTPol (AdvACT) multichroic detector arrays, which observed in frequency bands centered near 30, 40, 90, 150, and 220 GHz. The passbands were measured with a Fourier transform spectrometer (FTS) combined with coupling optics that direct and match the output of the FTS to the AdvACT receiver. We perform optical simulations of the FTS and coupling optics in order to model frequency-dependent systematic effects in this system, examining the systematics of each individual measurement component in detail. We use these simulations to apply corrections to the measurements and evaluate the remaining systematic uncertainty. We combine these systematic estimates with statistical errors to determine the measured passbands and their uncertainties from our FTS measurement, which are typically $0.75$ to $1.5\%$ per detector array for the central frequency. We present the passband characteristics for all measurements made by ACT in a common framework. Additionally, we discuss in detail limits set by the systematics in our measurements as well as ways to minimize the systematics of each component to improve passband measurements in the future.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Alford, Rahul Datta, Erminia Calabrese, Steve K. Choi, Shannon M. Duff, Adriaan J. Duivenvoorden, Rolando D\"unner, Joseph Golec, Matthew Hasselfeld, J. Colin Hill, Johannes Hubmayr, Jeffrey McMahon, Michael D. Niemack, Lyman A. Page, Suzanne T. Staggs, Alex Thomas, Cristian Vargas, Yuhan Wang, Edward J. Wollack

item.title: AI-Assisted Extraction of Follow-up Observations from GCN Circulars in Astro-COLIBRI
item.description: arXiv:2608.23270v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a new Astro-COLIBRI component that converts free-text GCN Circulars into structured, event-linked follow-up records and combines them with reports submitted directly by the community. A continuously running listener associates new Circulars with transient events, applies deterministic pre-analysis, and invokes a schema-constrained large language model to extract photometry, contacts, redshifts, and related metadata. The records are normalized into a common event-level database and exposed through the web and mobile interfaces as report summaries, contact tools, optical-afterglow context figures, and downloadable CSV or VOTable products. All 1,775 Circulars of an operational evaluation corpus covering the first half of 2026 completed the workflow without failures. An internal human audit of 210 Circulars found 223 of 231 assessed reports (96.5%) fully confirmed, each of the eight remaining ones containing at least one incorrect field, predominantly associated with observation timing and facility attribution. Extracted redshifts agree with three published compilations for 91.7 to 99.3% of the events they share, every disagreement tracing to a limit, a candidate-host estimate, or a later-refined value rather than to a misread Circular. The extraction also recovers 90 to 97% of the redshifts those compilations list for bursts it processed. Applied to the GCN archive since 2016, the pipeline yields 68,393 observations from 26,811 reports across 5,787 transient events, and now runs in real time on new Circulars. The reusable parsing and normalization pipeline is released as the open-source Python package astro-colibri-circular-parser.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific 138, 114505 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Fabian Sch\"ussler, S. Bisero, M. Cellier, A. Ciric, B. Cornejo, I. Jaroschewski, A. Kaan Alkan, W. Kiendr\'eb\'eogo, A. Saint-Paul

item.title: FAIR-Compliant Architecture for Heterogeneous Astronomical Data: KazVO Framework
item.description: arXiv:2609.39546v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents the architecture of the Kazakhstani National Virtual Observatory (KazVO) - an International Virtual Observatory Alliance (IVOA) compliant node that unifies the heterogeneous observational datasets of the Fesenkov Astrophysical Institute (FAI). The architectural foundation of the system is built upon a partitioned Data Lake, a German Astrophysical Virtual Observatory (GAVO) Data Center Helper Suite (DaCHS) publishing backend, and {a PostgreSQL database in which metadata for published observational products are mapped to IVOA ObsCore, while catalogs and simulation grids use dedicated relational tables}. We follow Open Science principles by introducing a metadata-only showcase model based on a four-class data embargo mechanism. Machine-to-Machine services deployed via IVOA protocols are exposed through the KazVO publishing registry registered in the global Registry of Registries (RofR), enabling analysis of Kazakhstani observational assets within external clients such as Tool for OPerations on Catalogues And Tables (TOPCAT), Aladin, and PyVO. The current implementation combines operational VO publication services and targeted photometric processing with scheduled, batch-mode data ingestion, supporting access to published historical and modern observational holdings. Replication has been validated on pilot datasets, while routine deployment at the observing sites and automated reduction of modern spectroscopic streams remain under development. The architecture provides a framework for progressively integrating these components into a complete data lifecycle.
item.dc:creator: Ildana Izmailova, Denis Yurin, Yerlan Aimuratov, Maxim Makukov, Aleksander Serebryanskiy, Saule Shomshekova, Vitaliy Kim, Chingis Omarov, Adel Umirbayeva, Laura Aktay, Dana Kuvatova, Anton Gluchshenko, Gulnara Suliyeva, Maxim Krugov, Nadezhda Vaidman, Daulet Anarbek, Inna Reva, Gauhar Aimanova, Rashit Valiullin, Raushan Kokumbayeva

item.title: Model of the instrumental polarization induced by a rotating HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures for CMB polarimetry
item.description: arXiv:2610.38165v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Future CMB polarization experiments require precise control of instrumental systematics in the search for primordial $B$-mode polarization. A rotating half-wave plate (HWP) provides effective polarization modulation, but its non-ideal electromagnetic response can generate HWP-synchronous instrumental polarization. In this work, we characterize the response of a multi-layer sapphire HWP with anti-reflective sub-wavelength structures (SWS) using rigorous coupled-wave analysis. For three asymmetric SWS models, we find no substantial differences in the transmittance, polarization efficiency, or instrumental-polarization response that can be attributed to the type of SWS asymmetry. The fourth-harmonic instrumental polarization relevant to CMB polarization reconstruction is typically of order $10^{-4}$ in the CMB bands, which is expected to be mitigated. We further evaluate an actually fabricated SWS geometry, whose asymmetry enhances the retardance, and compare its response with that of an idealized model having the same type of asymmetry. Comparison of the realistic SWS with the idealized model shows that higher transmittance tends to be associated with lower instrumental polarization. These results suggest that improving the total transmission, including the effect of the fabricated SWS profile, may be more important for reducing HWP-induced instrumental polarization than tuning the SWS asymmetry itself.
item.dc:creator: Ryota Takaku, Hiroaki Imada, Guillaume Patanchon, Yuki Sakurai

item.title: Benchmarking the expected performance of Bayesian parameter inference on Kilonovae
item.description: arXiv:2505.21392v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the study of optical transients, parameter inference is a part of the process of extracting physical information, i.e. constraints on the source's characteristics, by comparing the observed lightcurves to the predictions of different astrophysical models and finding the model and parameter combination that make the closest match. In the developing field of the study of kilonovae (KNe), systematic uncertainties in modeling are still very large. Current-day models still struggle to fit adequately the whole multi-wavelength dataset of the AT2017gfo kilonova, associated to the Binary Neutron Star (BNS) merger GW170817, and thus obtain wide posterior distributions on the inferred source parameters. After reviewing the many sources of uncertainty embedded in KN analyses and the process of Bayesian parameter inference, we discuss how to quantify the performance of parameter inference analyses using metrics on information gain from prior to posterior. We highlight the systematic error margin hyperparameter $\sigma_{\rm sys}$, which correlates to a model's goodness-of-fit, and exhibit its major influence on Bayesian inference performance metrics. Using the example of two KN models from the literature with the Nuclear Multi-Messenger Astronomy (NMMA) Bayesian inference framework, we simulate the expected information gains that dedicated KN follow-ups with telescope networks could reasonably reach, for various observational cadences and error margins: we show that the wind ejecta's mass and electron fraction are the easiest KN parameters to constrain. We finally apply our KN analysis to the dataset of AT2017gfo to show that our information gain predictions match results on real data and discuss the complementarity of multi-messenger approaches.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Hussenot-Desenonges (Universit\'e Paris-Saclay, CNRS/IN2P3, IJCLab), Marion Pillas (Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris, Sorbonne Universit\'e), Sarah Antier (Universit\'e Paris-Saclay, CNRS/IN2P3, IJCLab, Observatoire de la C\^ote d'Azur), Patrice Hello (Universit\'e Paris-Saclay, CNRS/IN2P3, IJCLab), Peter T. H. Pang (Nikhef, Institute for Gravitational and Subatomic Physics)

item.title: MarsRetrieval: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Planetary-Scale Geospatial Retrieval on Mars
item.description: arXiv:2602.13961v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data-driven approaches like deep learning are rapidly advancing planetary science, particularly in Mars exploration. Despite recent progress, most existing benchmarks remain confined to closed-set supervised visual tasks and do not support text-guided retrieval for geospatial discovery. We introduce MarsRetrieval, a retrieval benchmark for evaluating vision-language models for Martian geospatial discovery. MarsRetrieval includes three tasks: (1) paired image-text retrieval, (2) landform retrieval, and (3) global geo-localization, covering multiple spatial scales and diverse geomorphic origins. We propose a unified retrieval-centric protocol to benchmark multimodal embedding architectures, including contrastive dual-tower encoders and generative vision-language models. Our evaluation shows MarsRetrieval is challenging: even strong foundation models often fail to capture domain-specific geomorphic distinctions. We further show that domain-specific fine-tuning is critical for generalizable geospatial discovery in planetary settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml-stat-Sustech/MarsRetrieval
item.dc:creator: Shuoyuan Wang, Yiran Wang, Hongxin Wei

item.title: When Should Science Act on an Interstellar Anomaly?
item.description: arXiv:2604.20896v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An unusual interstellar object may warrant further observation even when there is little evidence that it is artificial. The challenge is deciding which observations are worth pursuing, how much to invest in them, and when to stop. We argue that the Loeb Scale can help guide these decisions, provided its levels are understood as provisional assessments rather than estimates of the probability of extraterrestrial technology. Candidate technosignature status may justify targeted follow-up when new observations could distinguish competing explanations and the expected scientific value warrants the cost. This requires testable predictions and retrodictions, attention to natural explanations not yet considered, and recognition of the risks of false alarms. We place this argument in the broader history and philosophy of scientific anomalies and relate it to existing assessment frameworks in SETI and astrobiology. The cases of 1I/Oumuamua, 2I/Borisov, and 3I/ATLAS illustrate why classifications and research priorities must remain open to revision. Candidate status is a reason to seek better evidence while it can still be obtained, not a conclusion about an object's origin.
item.dc:creator: Konrad Szocik, Abraham Loeb

item.title: HERMES: HiERarchical Modelling for Exoplanet Science
item.description: arXiv:2606.02696v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: ESA's Ariel Space Mission will characterise the atmospheres of approximately 1000 exoplanets to quantify population-level trends. We present HERMES (HiERarchical Modelling for Exoplanet Science), a multidimensional Bayesian framework that probes population-level correlations across multiple axes of diversity. The specific use case we present is the multidimensional relation between stellar metallicity, planetary mass, and atmospheric metallicity. Starting from the Ariel Mission Candidate Sample, we select confirmed planets with available masses and stellar metallicity, inject plausible multidimensional trends and demonstrate successful parameter recovery. Simulated surveys are generated with a variety of leverage and sample size, in the presence of intrinsic astrophysical scatter and measurement noise. By fitting independent Bayesian models to each survey, we confirm that survey leverage remains a reliable predictor of trend precision even in multiple dimensions and in the presence of intrinsic astrophysical scatter. For an Ariel Tier 2 transit survey of at least 400 planets, HERMES robustly recovers the correlation between stellar and planetary metallicity despite intrinsic scatter in planetary abundances as large as 1.2 dex. These results establish HERMES as a practical tool for survey design and science yield forecasting in preparation for Ariel and other surveys probing population-level trends.
item.dc:creator: Wasi M. F. Naqvi, Nicolas B. Cowan

item.title: SPLIT: Loosely-coherent inference of long-inspiral gravitational-wave sources for robustness against modeling and data outliers
item.description: arXiv:2606.13728v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves (GWs) from dozens of extreme- and intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs/IMRIs). These sources will stay in-band for months to years, offering extraordinary scientific potential. However, their fully phase-coherent analysis standard in current pipelines imposes stringent waveform accuracy requirements; failing to model the signal over such long durations can result in significant systematic biases. To address this, we formulate a robust Bayesian inference framework that segments the data into blocks, infers each block coherently, and recombines the results using loosely-coherent phase information. By restricting full phase-tracking to much shorter block durations, this approach prevents significant accumulation of phase errors. We implement this methodology in \textsc{SPLIT} (Segmented Posteriors for Long-Inspiral Templates), a GPU-accelerated Python package. Applying \textsc{SPLIT} to an environment-rich injection, we demonstrate that while a fully-coherent vacuum-GR analysis incurs a maximum 1D systematic bias of $\approx 4.8\sigma$ from the truth, the shorter integration window of our loosely-coherent approach restricts such biases to $\lesssim 0.5\sigma$. Overall, despite a fractional loss of optimal signal-to-noise ratio, the substantial improvement in parameter accuracy offered by our method presents a highly advantageous trade-off for LISA and other future GW detectors.
item.dc:creator: Shubham Kejriwal

item.title: A comparison of particle and fluid approaches for modeling the streaming instability in global patch simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.09575v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Identifying the process relevant to planet formation is still a major task. Mechanisms have been identified that can trap dust, preventing it from migrating inwards. A particular hydrodynamic instability, known as the streaming instability, is of high interest because it may be responsible for the formation of dust clumps from which the first planetesimals form. We aim to compare the outcome of non-linear streaming instability simulations using both fundamental approaches in a more realistic global disk model. The results will not be used to identify or disentangle the effect of, e.g., numerical diffusion in fluid simulations or the possibility of having crossing particle streams. Instead, they will enable us to determine whether the Lagrangian particle approach is the most suitable for numerical studies of the streaming instability. Methods: We perform 2D, axisymmetric, global, and isothermal hydrodynamic simulations using the two codes FARGO3D (dust fluid) and PLUTO (fluid, particles) to investigate the temporal evolution of dust scale height, midplane dust-to-gas ratio, and maximum dust density as well as to study velocity distributions and vorticities. For PLUTO particle simulations, we also investigate the influence of the gas Riemann solver and spatial reconstruction orders. Our results from a resolution study up to 5120 cells per gas scale height indicate convergence between PLUTO fluid and FARGO3D. Both yield a Gaussian profile dominated by small-scale, dust-depleted voids. Particle simulations with PLUTO have not yet converged, as a transient midplane dust component persists, indicating the need for even higher resolution or more particles. Using a more accurate Riemann solver or a higher-order spatial reconstruction scheme helps to bring the dust density profile closer to the converged structure.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Hetzel Ostertag, Mario Flock, Paul Rosendahl, Andrea Mignone, Jeonghoon Lim, Jacob B. Simon

item.title: Millimeter-Wavelength Constraints on Circular Polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background at Arcminute Scales with the Simons Array
item.description: arXiv:2611.13345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present constraints on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) circular polarization anisotropy at arcminute angular scales, using dedicated measurements from the Simons Array taken with a quarter-wave plate and rotating half-wave plate. A detection of circular polarization in the CMB would probe a range of proposed generation mechanisms, from Standard Model astrophysics to physics beyond it. At an observing frequency of 90 GHz, we place constraints over the multipole range $300 \leq \ell \leq 2000$, corresponding to angular scales of 5.4-36 arcmin, in bands of width $\Delta \ell = 100$, roughly tripling the highest multipole previously reached by a $V$-mode power spectrum measurement. Within this domain, we constrain the 95% confidence upper bound of $\ell (\ell+1) C_\ell^{VV} / (2\pi)$ to range from $\sim 22\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 350$ bandpower to $\sim 3.5 \times 10^3\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 1950$ bandpower. These limits are derived from $\sim$2.5 months of observations of each of two small regions of the sky located away from the Galactic plane, totaling $\sim$12 deg$^2$ of effective sky area. Because the methodology of this study marginalizes known foreground contamination, these bounds serve as robust, conservative limits on the true CMB circular polarization signal down to the sensitivity limits of the instrument. Additionally, we provide an experimental and analytical framework for implementing circular polarization observations on other telescopes by utilizing a quarter-wave plate and half-wave plate design.

item.title: New Constraints on the Ultrahigh Energy Neutrino Flux from the First Array-Wide Search with the Askaryan Radio Array
item.description: arXiv:2611.14350v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ultrahigh energy neutrinos ($E_\nu \gtrsim 100$ PeV) are detectable through Askaryan emission---the nanosecond-scale radio impulse emitted by relativistic particle cascades in a dielectric medium. The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA), an Askaryan detector array located at the South Pole, has been taking data for more than a decade. We present the first array-wide search for diffuse ultrahigh energy neutrinos with ARA. The search found no events on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. The resulting upper limit is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV and provides the first constraints on the flux reported by the KM3NeT Collaboration that are complementary to optical Cherenkov and particle detectors. This limit also constrains UHECR source models, and excludes some models with trans-GZK proton populations at the $90\%$ confidence level. This represents the largest Askaryan detector dataset ever analyzed, demonstrating the feasibility and sensitivity of searches with large detector arrays acting as a single observatory. It also underscores the high acceptance and exposure of Askaryan detector arrays to ultrahigh energy neutrinos.

item.title: Analysis Methodology of the Search for Ultrahigh Energy Neutrinos in 10.6 Years of Askaryan Radio Array Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.14354v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) is an in-ice radio observatory at the South Pole designed to detect ultrahigh energy (UHE) neutrinos through Askaryan emission produced by interactions of neutrinos and their secondary particles. In this paper, we present the detailed methodology of the first array-wide search for a diffuse UHE neutrino flux using data from all five ARA stations. The dataset considered represents $10.6$ years of livetime and is three times larger than previous ARA neutrino searches. This search achieves a $28\%$ analysis efficiency for a neutrino flux corresponding to the current experimental upper limits. No neutrino candidates are observed on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. We set a new upper limit on the diffuse UHE neutrino flux, which is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV. We also discuss lessons learned for future searches on large radio arrays.
